# Gāmaṇi Saṁyutta (SN 42)

**ID:** SN 42
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Gāmaṇi Saṁyutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Linked Discourses with Chiefs
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/sn42
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0304m.mul7.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Gāmaṇisaṁyutta* (SN 42) is the forty-second chapter of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated within the *Saḷāyatanavagga* [Bodhi 2003; Jerryson et al. 2017]. The collection comprises thirteen discourses centered on conversations between the Buddha and various village headmen or chieftains (*gāmaṇi*) [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003]. Many of the interlocutors represent specialized occupations—such as the mercenary commander Yodhājīva, horse trainers, and the actor-manager Tālapuṭa—or seek out the Buddha with adversarial intent, attempting to debate him or questioning whether monastics should accept gold and silver [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003; Jerryson et al. 2017]. Key topics discussed include the karmic destiny of warriors and performers, the futility of brahmanical funeral rituals, the cultivation of loving-kindness, and craving as the root of suffering (as illustrated through the sorrow that arises from attachment to loved ones in SN 42.11) [SuttaCentral; Flores 2008; Jerryson et al. 2017]. In each case, the Buddha gently dispels their preconceptions through measured reasoning and ethical analysis [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003].

Twelve discourses in the collection possess parallels across Chinese and northern Buddhist collections, primarily within the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) and the "Alternative" *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 100), with two discourses (SN 42.6 and SN 42.13) paralleled in the *Madhyama Āgama* (T 26, MĀ 17 and MĀ 20) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus corroborates these alignments and also detects textual alignments with the Mūlasarvāstivāda *Vinayavastu*, the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu*, and the *Arthaviniścayasūtra* [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, the collection shares substantial text reuse with the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (especially between SN 42.12 and AN 10.91 on righteous and unrighteous livelihoods) as well as *Majjhimanikāya* discourses (MN 60, MN 76) and the *Nettippakaraṇa* [DharmaNexus; Bodhi 2012].

In modern scholarship, the *Gāmaṇisaṁyutta* is widely cited in discussions of early Buddhist perspectives on warfare and state violence [Bartholomeusz 2002; Jerryson et al. 2017]. In particular, the Buddha's rejection in SN 42.3 of the belief that fallen soldiers attain heaven—pointing out that killing in battle stems from debased, hostile intentions leading to lower rebirth—has served as a foundational proof text for scholars analyzing early Buddhist anti-war ethics [Bartholomeusz 2002; Jerryson et al. 2017]. Additionally, the trumpeter simile (*saṅkhadhama*) in SN 42.8 illustrates the boundless nature of the immeasurable mental liberations (*appamāṇa*), a formulation examined in discussions of Buddhist meditation practice and later scholastic treatises [IABU 2012].

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral entry for SN 42 — Structure, English title, themes of headmen debates, and parallel concordances across SA, SA2, and MA.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus machine match database for SN 42 — Pali-internal text reuse (AN 10, MN 60, MN 76) and cross-language alignments with Chinese Āgamas, Sanskrit Vinaya, and Tibetan texts.

- [Bartholomeusz 2002] Tessa J. Bartholomeusz, In Defence of Dharma: Just-war ideology in Buddhist Sri Lanka (2002) — Scholarly debate regarding Schmithausen's use of the Gāmaṇi Saṁyutta as a proof text against warfare.
- [Jerryson et al. 2017] Michael K. Jerryson, Mark Juergensmeyer, and Margo Kitts, Violence and the World's Religious Traditions: An Introduction (2017) — Discussion of SN 42.3 (Yodhājīva) regarding warrior ethics and karmic intention.
- [Bodhi 2012] Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Numerical Discourses of the Buddha: A Complete Translation of the Aṅguttara Nikāya (2012) — Comparison of the grouping of grounds for praise and blame between SN 42.12 and AN parallels.
